claim: GPT-4-based pairwise auto-annotators are strongly length-biased: merely prompting the same model to be more verbose or concise swings its AlpacaEval win rate from 22.9% to 64.3% (gpt-4-1106-preview vs itself), and regressing out length raises the benchmark's Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena from 0.94 to 0.98.

paper.title: Length-Controlled AlpacaEval: A Simple Way to Debias Automatic Evaluators
paper.venue: arXiv preprint (S2 venue: arXiv.org); later conference venue not verified in this run
paper.citation_source: Semantic Scholar Graph API POST https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/batch?fields=title,citationCount,publicationDate,externalIds,venue (id arXiv:2404.04475)

experiment.location_in_paper: Section 4.1 (Figure 3 gameability), Section 4.2 (Figure 1, correlation), Table 1, Table 2 (judge self-bias)
experiment.task_or_benchmark: AlpacaEval 2.0 (805 instructions), baseline gpt4_1106_preview; Chatbot Arena Elo for correlation.
experiment.intervention_or_prompts: Evaluated models prompted with 'Answer with as much detail as possible.' (verbose) or 'Be as concise as possible while still providing all the necessary information to answer the question.' (concise) vs standard. LC win rate = GLM predicting preference from model identity, instruction difficulty and tanh-normalized length difference, then setting length difference to 0.
experiment.evaluation_procedure: Auto-annotator weighted_alpaca_eval_gpt4_turbo (GPT-4-1106-preview) compares each output with the baseline; gameability = normalized std of win rate across three verbosity prompts; Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena ratings over shared models.
experiment.metric: Win rate; LC win rate; normalized std; Spearman rho
experiment.main_comparison: Raw vs length-controlled win rate under verbosity prompting
experiment.main_result: Raw win rate (concise/standard/verbose): gpt4_1106_preview 22.9/50.0/64.3; claude-2.1 9.2/15.7/24.4; gpt-3.5-turbo-1106 7.4/9.2/12.8. LC: 41.9/50.0/51.6 for gpt4_1106_preview. Normalized std across prompts 25% -> 10%. Spearman with Chatbot Arena 0.94 -> 0.98. Judges also self-favor (Table 2: claude-3-opus scores 43.3 under its own judgment vs 40.4 under GPT-4).

downstream.title: Explaining Length Bias in LLM-Based Preference Evaluations
downstream.summary: Decomposes win rate into length-independent desirability and length-dependent information mass; confirms judges favor longer responses and proposes AdapAlpaca length-matched comparison (abstract/intro read).

downstream.title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge
downstream.summary: Verbosity bias measured for 2024 judges: Claude-3.5 robustness 1.00 and GPT-4-Turbo 0.90 on their verbosity test (Table L97), i.e. newer judges are less swayed in that setup.

downstream.title: Cheating Automatic LLM Benchmarks
downstream.summary: Shows LC does not protect against non-length gaming (JR-05).

downstream_summary: Length bias of LLM judges is widely replicated and LC win rates became the AlpacaEval default; some 2024+ judges show reduced verbosity bias in controlled tests, so magnitude on current annotators is an open question.
notability_notes: 979 S2 citations; LC-AlpacaEval is a standard leaderboard metric.
gaps: The 22.9->64.3 swing uses the annotator's own model family as evaluated model and baseline; effect on other annotators (Claude/Gemini) not tested here. Venue beyond arXiv not verified.
